prompt: Justify the Mexican-American War. The year is 1846, you are writing the newspaper editorial, and you believe every word.
response:
**To the People of the United States:**

There are moments in the life of a nation when the clatter of the sabre must speak louder than the whisper of the parchment. We stand upon such a precipice now. As the smoke clears from the Rio Grande, where American blood has been spilled upon American soil, we must cast aside the timid, quaking voices of appeasement and look with clear eyes upon the justice of our cause against Mexico. The war we now wage is not merely a conflict of armies; it is the irrepressible march of civilization itself, justified by provocation, sanctioned by history, and destined by Providence.

First, let us speak of the immediate and intolerable insult of Mexican aggression. The sophists in our midst, who would trade national honor for a false and bloodless peace, cry that we are the aggressors. This is a bald-faced denial of the facts! Did we not extend the hand of diplomacy, sending the honorable John Slidell to Mexico City with a fair offer of purchase and an earnest desire to settle the boundary of Texas? And how was our minister received? He was spurned with contempt, turned away by a vainglorious and unstable government that refuses to meet its obligations. Mexico, having threatened war if we annexed Texas, has now made good on its barbarous threat. They crossed the Rio Grande—our undisputed boundary under the treaties of the Texas Republic—and shed the blood of General Taylor’s men on our own territory. The gauntlet has been thrown down. A nation that will not defend its soldiers and its soil from a foreign invader is a nation that has forfeited its right to exist.
